description: This topic under General Science covers the study of the motion of objects and the forces acting upon them. It is a highly crucial section for competitive exams, focusing on fundamental principles, mathematical relationships, and real-world applications.

sections.title: Fundamental Concepts of Kinematics
sections.description: Basic physical quantities used to describe the motion of an object in physics.

key_concepts.explanation: The total length of the path covered by an object. It is a scalar quantity and can never be zero or negative if an object has moved.
The shortest distance between the initial and final positions of a moving object. It is a vector quantity and can be positive, negative, or zero.
The rate of change of displacement with respect to time. Its SI unit is meters per second (m/s), and it is a vector quantity.
The rate of change of velocity with respect to time. Its SI unit is m/s². A decrease in velocity over time is called retardation or deceleration.

sections.title: Equations of Motion
sections.description: Mathematical equations formulated by Galileo and Newton for objects moving with uniform acceleration in a straight line.

scientific_principles.application: Establishes the relationship between velocity and time. It is used to calculate the final velocity (v) when initial velocity (u), acceleration (a), and time (t) are given.
Establishes the relationship between position and time. It is used to calculate the total distance covered or displacement (s).
Establishes the relationship between position and velocity. It is useful when the time (t) factor is not provided in a problem.

sections.title: Newton's Laws of Motion
sections.description: Three fundamental laws compiled by Sir Isaac Newton in his book 'Principia' that describe the relationship between a body and the forces acting upon it.

key_concepts.explanation: The inherent property of a body by virtue of which it resists any change in its state of rest or uniform motion. Inertia is directly proportional to the mass of the body.
The product of the mass and velocity of an object (p = mv). It is a vector quantity indicating the quantity of motion contained in a body.

scientific_principles.formula_or_statement: An object will remain at rest or in uniform motion in a straight line unless acted upon by an external unbalanced force.
scientific_principles.application: A passenger leaning backward when a stationary bus suddenly starts moving, or dust flying off a carpet when beaten with a stick.

scientific_principles.formula_or_statement: The rate of change of momentum of a body is directly proportional to the applied force and takes place in the direction of the force (F = ma).
scientific_principles.application: A cricket fielder pulling his hands backward while catching a fast-moving ball to increase the time of impact and reduce the force.

scientific_principles.formula_or_statement: To every action, there is always an equal and opposite reaction.
scientific_principles.application: The recoil of a gun when a bullet is fired, and the upward thrust experienced by a rocket during launch.

sections.title: Friction and Circular Motion
sections.description: Study of opposing forces between contact surfaces and the dynamics of objects moving in curved paths.

key_concepts.explanation: The opposing force that comes into play when two surfaces are in contact and attempt to move relative to each other. Limiting friction is the maximum value of static friction.
The required inward force that keeps an object moving in a circular path, directed towards the center of rotation.
A pseudo or fictitious force that appears to act radially outward on a body moving in a circular path, observed from a rotating reference frame.

scientific_principles.application: The Earth revolving around the Sun, and a cyclist leaning inwards while negotiating a sharp turn.

sections.title: Exam-Oriented Important Facts
sections.description: Crucial one-liner facts, direct mappings, and superlative data points frequently asked in competitive exams.

important_facts.fact: The standard value of acceleration due to gravity (g) on the surface of the Earth is 9.8 m/s².
The value of 'g' is minimum at the Earth's equator and maximum at the poles.

In a perfect vacuum, all objects falling freely experience the exact same acceleration, regardless of their size, shape, or mass.
